implementation_notes: TypeScript adds the static layer to the same array methods: map infers the result element type from the callback, filter has a type-predicate overload (xs.filter((x): x is T => ...)) that narrows the result, and reduce needs the accumulator type to unify (usually via an explicit generic argument). The handbook's generic-function guidance applies directly to pipeline stages - prefer the type parameter itself over a constraint and use as few type parameters as possible, otherwise inference collapses inside the callback. This replaces the manual typed loop and is the default realization; the untyped array form is the same runtime.
pitfalls: filter without a type predicate returns the source element type: xs.filter(x => x !== null) still has type (T | null)[] unless the callback declares a type predicate.
reduce infers the accumulator from the initial value, so a missing generic silently widens the result (or fails) with the error pointing at the reducer, not the stage.
Long chains make the compiler re-check every callback: naming the intermediate types keeps inference fast and errors local.

variants.name: Typed lazy iterables and generator pipelines
variants.idiom_name: Generator<T> / IterableIterator<T> stages (+ lib esnext.iterator helper types)
variants.implementation_notes: For lazy typing TypeScript follows the runtime: Iterable<T>/IterableIterator<T> and generator functions (function*(): Generator<T>) describe a pull-based pipeline, and the handbook's iterator chapter warns that when targeting an ES5 engine 'iterators are only allowed on values of Array type', so --downlevelIteration (or an ES2015+ target) is required to keep the iterator protocol in the emitted code. The iterator-helper methods are typed in lib.esnext.iterator (Iterator.prototype.map/filter plus IteratorObject), so a truly lazy chain can be typed end to end - but the target and lib settings, not the types, decide whether the runtime actually has them.
pitfalls: Types erase: the lazy-versus-eager distinction and iterator-helper availability are runtime properties, so code typed against lib.esnext.iterator compiles and then fails on an older Node/browser.
A value typed as Iterable<T> may be a single-use Generator<T>: the interface hides that a second traversal yields nothing.
Without downlevelIteration (or with an ES5 target) for...of over non-array iterables is a compile error, and the emitted helper's semantics differ from the native protocol.
